Monolithic kernels run scheduling, memory management, device drivers, file systems, and networking in one privileged address space with low-overhead direct calls.
Linux and traditional Unix use monolithic kernels and still dominate many production systems.
A bug in a tightly coupled monolithic module can crash the entire machine, and the shared codebase can be harder to maintain or secure.
Microkernels typically retain IPC, basic scheduling, and low-level memory control in privileged mode while running drivers, file systems, and higher services in user-space servers.
Microkernel isolation can allow individual services to be restarted or swapped without bringing down the system.
Microkernel context switches and IPC overhead historically hurt performance, but modern designs have narrowed the gap.
Many systems use hybrid kernels that keep performance-critical components in kernel space while modularizing other services.
